study.title: 1 Samuel 15 The rejection of Saul for disobeying the word of the LORD
study.overview: This chapter tells the decisive proof of Saul's obedience. The Lord, through Samuel, commands judgment against Amalek for his former cruelty against Israel. Saul gets military victory, but spares Aggag and the best of the flock, claiming that the spoil would be used in sacrifice. Samuel confronts Saul and shows that obedience is worth more than the religious ritual. The narrative ends with the confirmation of Saul's rejection as king: Samuel departs from him, laments his fall, and the LORD declares that Saul's choice would not be maintained.

outline.title: The Order of Destroying Amalek and Saul's Partial Obedition
outline.explanation: Samuel recalls that it was the LORD who placed Saul on the throne and now gives him a specific command: to execute judgment against Amalek for his historical hostility against Israel. Saul gathers troops, spares the Natives because of the goodness that they showed Israel, overcomes the Amalekites, but preserves Agag and the best of the flock, destroying only what he considered weak and worthless.

outline.title: Samuel announces divine reprobation and corrects false religiosity
outline.explanation: The LORD reveals to Samuel that Saul departed and did not fulfill the word received. Samuel goes to meet Saul, who tries to say that he obeyed, but is confronted by the sound of the spared animals. Saul's answer exposes his justification: he attributes the decision to the people and to an alleged sacrificial use of the spoil. Samuel then declares the central principle of the chapter: to obey it is better than to sacrifice, and rejecting the word of the LORD is equivalent to rebellion and idolatry; therefore Saul is rejected as king.

outline.title: Late confession, final sentence and mourning Samuel
outline.explanation: Saul admits sin, but his words show concern for public honor and not a profound change of heart. Samuel refuses to return with him and reaffirms that the kingdom was plucked from Saul and given to another. The chapter concludes with the execution of Agag, the definitive separation between Samuel and Saul, and the lament of the prophet, while the text states that the LORD was grieved for having put Saul as king.

study.context: The text alludes to previous episodes of Israel's story in which Amalek attacked the Israelites during the exit of Egypt. The order of judgment is linked to this memory of the covenant and divine justice. Also appear the Cheruss, spared by their attitude favorable to Israel in the exodus, showing that the chapter distinguishes between enemies of the people and those who treated Israel with mercy. The scenario is the period of the initial monarchy, with Saul already established as king, but now valued for his faithfulness to the word received.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that authority received from God continues to be subordinate to the word of God. The king of Israel cannot use military success, religious intent, or popular pressure as an excuse to disobey. The sacrifice, no matter as noble as it may seem, does not replace obedience. The narrative also shows that divine judgment is morally serious: God treats Amalek's violence as a real guilt and treats Saul's disobedience as infidelity of covenant. At the same time, Samuel's sorrow reveals the pain of rejection and the spiritual weight of a failed reign. The phrase about the Lord must be read, in the light of the notes, as a change of action and administration in the face of Saul's change, not as a moral error or instability in God.

scholarViews.insight: The chapter shows that Saul's rejection becomes stronger because he did not fully obey the commandment to destroy the Amalekites.
Saul's disobedience was aggravated because God's command was a clear test of obedience.
The remembrance of what Amalek did to Israel explains that the judgment now executed is linked to the ancient cruelty against the people at its exit from Egypt.

questions: When I justify disobedience by saying that my intention was good, am I really listening to the word of God?
In what situations can I be preferring religious appearance, service or results, rather than simple obedience to the Lord?
What does my reaction to the confrontation reveal: true regret or just concern for my image?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to obey in whole, not selective. Examine areas in which you have preserved what God has abandoned, perhaps out of fear of people, for personal interest or spiritual convenience. Confect with sincerity any disobedience, without using godly excuses. Also learn from Samuel to take the word of God seriously and to mourn, in prayer, when leaders and believers exchange obedience for religious appearance. This week's concrete application is to identify a biblical order that you already know, but have postponed, and practice it in an objective way.
study.uncertainty: The text and notes allow us to safely affirm the general meaning of "repentance" applied to God as a change of action or administrative disposition, but do not explain exhaustively how this relates to divine immutability. It is also not possible, based only on the given notes, to accurately determine who would be the best mentioned by Samuel.
